meta.title: Who really said "Get in good trouble, necessary trouble"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — John Lewis really said it. “Good trouble, necessary trouble” is verbatim in his 2018 tweet and his final 2020 New York Times essay.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Get in good trouble, necessary trouble'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely John Lewis. His signature phrase appears verbatim in a 2018 tweet and his posthumous 2020 New York Times essay.

answer.label: Spoken & written by
answer.sourceLine: This is one of the rare cases where the famous name really said it. “Good trouble” was John Lewis’s lifelong catchphrase, and the pairing “good trouble, necessary trouble” appears verbatim in his 27 June 2018 tweet and in his final essay, published in The New York Times on the day of his funeral, 30 July 2020.

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: “Together, You Can Redeem the Soul of Our Nation”
The New York Times, 30 July 2020 (written before his death on 17 July 2020)

source.excerpt: Ordinary people with extraordinary vision can redeem the soul of America by getting in what I call good trouble, necessary trouble. Voting and participating in the democratic process are key.
trail: Wikiquote sources the wording to Lewis’s June 2018 tweet, quoted in USA Today’s 18 July 2020 tribute headline “‘Get in good trouble, necessary trouble.’”
The Bill of Rights Institute primary-source packet reproduces the New York Times essay verbatim, including “getting in what I call good trouble, necessary trouble.”

Lewis traced “good trouble” to his youth: told by elders not to get into trouble, he chose to make “good trouble, necessary trouble” instead — a phrase he used across decades of speeches and interviews.
source.excerptNote: From Lewis’s posthumously published essay. In his 2018 tweet the phrase appears in the imperative form the slogan is drawn from: “Never, ever be afraid to make some noise and get in good trouble, necessary trouble.”

source.rightsHolder: Estate of John Lewis; The New York Times Company (essay)
source.rightsNote: The wording is drawn from work first published in 2018 (tweet) and 2020 (the New York Times essay), so it is in copyright in the United States. The three-word slogan on its own is likely too short to be independently protectable, but the sentences it comes from belong to Lewis’s estate and his publisher.

author.name: John Lewis
author.heading: About John Lewis
author.bio: John Robert Lewis was an American civil rights leader and politician who chaired SNCC, spoke at the 1963 March on Washington, and was beaten leading the 1965 Selma march across the Edmund Pettus Bridge. He represented Georgia in Congress from 1987 until his death in 2020, and made “good trouble, necessary trouble” his enduring call to nonviolent activism.

misattribution.heading: Genuine — but often condensed
misattribution.intro: Unlike most feel-good lines pinned on famous names, this one is authentic. The main thing to get right is the wording and where the neat slogan comes from.

items.who: A condensation of Lewis’s own longer sentences
items.why: Lewis’s documented lines are “get in good trouble, necessary trouble” (within his 2018 tweet) and “getting in what I call good trouble, necessary trouble” (2020 essay). The clipped three-word imperative was popularized as the title of the 2020 documentary and the USA Today tribute headline.
Lewis did not coin the phrase in one famous address; he used “good trouble” across decades, tracing it to childhood elders who warned him not to get into trouble.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are authentically John Lewis’s — a phrase he used for decades and placed in his final essay, published the day of his funeral in The New York Times.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: For John Lewis, “good trouble” distilled a lifetime of nonviolent direct action — sit-ins, Freedom Rides, and the march across the Edmund Pettus Bridge — into a permission slip for ordinary people to break unjust rules on purpose.

He returned to the phrase constantly in his final years, and chose to close his life with it: his farewell essay urges the next generation to redeem the nation “by getting in what I call good trouble, necessary trouble.”
